full_judgment:
"The necessary parties in a suit for specific performance of a contract for sale are the parties to the contract, or if they are dead their legal representatives, as also a person who had purchased the property from the vendor after the contract. He is necessary party as lie would be affected, if he is a volunteer, or if a purchaser for value, had purchased with notice of the contract. A person who claims adversely to the Vendor is however, not a necessary party. Where the property stands in the name of person other then the vender, and the suit for specific performance is brought by the purchaser, that person may be joined as a defendant as a proper party on an allegation that he is the benamidar of the vendor but if he appears and contends that he is not the benamidar of the vendor the proper procedure would be to discharge him from the suit, leaving it to the plaintiff in the suit for specific performance to institute a suit against him after he had got the conveyance in execution of the decree for specific performance against his Vendor. This is on the principle that the scope of a suit for specific performance of a contract also ought not to be enlarged and the suit turned also into a title "Suit between one of either of the parties to the contract and a stranger to the contract." 

 "Specific performance of contract may be enforced under section 27 against either party to the contract or any other person claiming under him by a title arising subsequently to the contract. In view of this provision in section 27 a prior purchaser ought to impaled a subsequent purchaser as a party to the suit for specific performance, because he is a necessary party inasmuch as, by a decree in favour of the prior purchaser the subsequent purchaser's right in the property is effected since if the sale deed executed by the seller in favour of the prior purchaser is registered, it being of a prior date to the sale in favour of the subsequent purchaser, his title to the land will be immediately affected by it." 

 “...The property cannot be transferred or otherwise dealt with by any party to the suit or proceeding so as to affect the rights of any other party thereto under any decree or order which may be made there under......” 

 8. The next case relied upon by Mr. Gafur is that of Fazar Ali vs Abut Kasem Shaikh 22 DLR 240. The facts have no resemblance with the facts of the instant case. The learned Single Judge took the view in the facts of that case alone and the principle cannot be applied in the facts of the instant case. The last case cited by Mr Gufar is the case of Lala Durga Prasad and another vs Lala Deep Chand reported in 1954 SC 934. In this case a subsequent purchaser was impleaded by the plaintiff in a suit for specific performance of a contract. The question arose, what should be the form of the decree since the practice of the courts in India was not uniform. It was held that the proper form of the decree was to direct specific performance of the contract between the vendor and the plaintiff and direct the subsequent transferee to join the conveyance so as to pass the title, which resides in him to the plaintiff. This principle would have applied if the subsequent transfer was made before the institution of the suit by the plaintiff for specific performance of the contract between plaintiff and his vendor. In such a case the subsequent purchaser will be a necessary party for securing complete title in the event of plaintiff's success in the suit. In the instant case, the subsequent transfer took place during the pendency of the plaintiff's suit for specific performance of the Contract against his vendor. These are all the decisions which Mr. Gafur wished us to consider in support of his contention.
